title: McCulloch and Pitts model the first artificial neuron
one_liner: A neuron described as simple logic: inputs add up, and it fires past a threshold.
summary: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts showed that networks of very simple on/off units could compute logical functions. It is the first mathematical model of a neuron and the starting point of neural networks.

sources.title: A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity

notes: Crossref: A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity [[1943, 12], [1943, 12]]

title: Turing asks: can machines think?
one_liner: Alan Turing replaces 'can machines think' with a test: can a machine pass as human in conversation?
summary: In 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Turing proposed the imitation game, now called the Turing test, and answered objections to machine intelligence that are still argued today.

sources.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence

notes: Crossref: I.—COMPUTING MACHINERY AND INTELLIGENCE [[1950, 10, 1], [1950, 10, 1], [1950, 10, 1]]

title: The Dartmouth proposal names the field 'artificial intelligence'
one_liner: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon propose a summer study and coin the term 'artificial intelligence'.
summary: The proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth summer workshop argued that every aspect of learning could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. The workshop is usually treated as the founding of AI.

sources.title: A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

notes: page loads (200):

title: Rosenblatt's perceptron learns from examples
one_liner: A machine that adjusts its own weights from labelled examples: the first learning neural network.
summary: Frank Rosenblatt described the perceptron, a single-layer network with a learning rule that updates weights after each mistake. It could learn simple visual patterns and drew huge public attention.

sources.title: The perceptron: A probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain

notes: Crossref: The perceptron: A probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. [[1958], [1958]]

title: Arthur Samuel's checkers program learns to play
one_liner: A program improves at checkers by playing itself, and the phrase 'machine learning' enters use.
summary: Arthur Samuel at IBM built a checkers player that improved through self-play and stored experience. His paper popularised the term machine learning: getting computers to learn without being explicitly programmed.

sources.title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers

notes: Crossref: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers [[1959, 7], [1959, 7]]

title: ELIZA, the first chatbot
one_liner: A simple pattern-matching program at MIT convinces some users it understands them.
summary: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA rephrased user input using keyword rules, most famously as a psychotherapist. People attributed understanding to it, an effect now called the ELIZA effect.

sources.title: ELIZA: a computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine

notes: Crossref: ELIZA—A Computer Program For the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine [[1966, 1, 1], [1966, 1, 1], [1966, 1, 1]]

title: The Lighthill report triggers the first AI winter
one_liner: A UK government review concludes AI has failed its promises, and funding is cut.
summary: James Lighthill's report for the UK Science Research Council criticised the lack of real-world results from AI research. Funding cuts in the UK and later the US followed, a period known as the first AI winter.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey (Lighthill report)

notes: page loads (200): Chilton::INF::Lighthill Report

title: Hopfield networks store memories
one_liner: A network that settles into stored patterns, recalling a whole memory from a partial cue.
summary: John Hopfield showed how a recurrent network with symmetric connections can act as associative memory, linking neural networks to physics. This work was part of his 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.title: Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities

notes: Crossref: Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities. [[1982, 4], [1982, 4], [1982, 4]]

title: Backpropagation popularised for training multi-layer networks
one_liner: A way to share the blame for an error across every layer, so deep networks can learn.
summary: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed that backpropagating errors lets networks with hidden layers learn useful internal representations. Nearly every neural network trained today still uses this method.

sources.title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors

notes: Crossref: Learning representations by back-propagating errors [[1986, 10], [1986, 10]]

title: LeCun applies convolutional networks to handwritten digits
one_liner: A network with shared filters reads handwritten zip codes for the US postal service.
summary: Yann LeCun and colleagues at Bell Labs trained a convolutional network with backpropagation to recognise handwritten digits. It is the direct ancestor of the networks that later won ImageNet.

sources.title: Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition

notes: Crossref: Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition [[1989, 12], [1989, 12]]

title: Q-learning gets its convergence proof
one_liner: An agent learns the value of each action by trial and error, with no model of the world.
summary: Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in his 1989 thesis, and the 1992 paper with Peter Dayan proved it converges. Deep Q-networks used it to play Atari games in 2013.

sources.title: Q-learning

notes: Crossref: Q-learning [[1992, 5], [1992, 5]]

title: TD-Gammon reaches expert backgammon by self-play
one_liner: A neural network teaches itself backgammon by playing against itself.
summary: Gerald Tesauro's TD-Gammon combined temporal-difference learning with a neural network and reached the level of top human players, an early success for self-play reinforcement learning.

sources.title: Temporal difference learning and TD-Gammon

notes: Crossref: Temporal difference learning and TD-Gammon [[1995, 3], [1995, 3], [1995, 3]]

title: Support vector machines
one_liner: A classifier that draws the widest possible margin between classes.
summary: Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik introduced support-vector networks, which dominated many classification tasks for the next 15 years thanks to strong theory and good results on small data.

sources.title: Support-vector networks

notes: Crossref: Support-vector networks [[1995, 9], [1995, 9]]

title: Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov
one_liner: IBM's chess computer wins a six-game match against the reigning world champion.
summary: Deep Blue relied on special chess hardware and brute-force search rather than learning. Its win showed that machines could beat the best humans at a game long seen as a test of intelligence.

sources.title: Deep Blue (IBM history)

notes: page loads (200): Deep Blue | IBM

title: Long short-term memory (LSTM)
one_liner: A recurrent network with gates that decide what to remember and what to forget.
summary: Sepp Hochreiter and Jurgen Schmidhuber solved the vanishing gradient problem for recurrent networks with gated memory cells. LSTMs powered speech recognition and translation until transformers arrived.

sources.title: Long Short-Term Memory

notes: Crossref: Long Short-Term Memory [[1997, 11, 1], [1997, 11, 1]]

title: LeNet-5 and gradient-based document recognition
one_liner: The classic convolutional network design, used to read cheques at scale.
summary: LeCun, Bottou, Bengio and Haffner described LeNet-5 and an end-to-end system for reading documents. The MNIST dataset from this work became the 'hello world' of machine learning.

sources.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition

notes: Crossref: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition [[1998], [1998]]

title: Random forests
one_liner: Many decision trees vote, and the crowd beats any single tree.
summary: Leo Breiman's random forests combined bagging with random feature selection. They remain a strong default for tabular data, the kind analysts work with every day.

sources.title: Random Forests

notes: Crossref: Random Forests [[2001, 10], [2001, 10]]

title: A neural probabilistic language model
one_liner: A neural network predicts the next word and learns word vectors along the way.
summary: Yoshua Bengio and colleagues trained a network to predict the next word, learning a vector for each word at the same time. This idea of learned embeddings runs through every modern language model.

sources.title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (JMLR)

title: Deep belief nets revive deep learning
one_liner: Training deep networks one layer at a time finally works.
summary: Hinton, Osindero and Teh showed a fast greedy way to pre-train deep networks layer by layer. It restarted interest in deep networks and gave 'deep learning' its name.

sources.title: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets

notes: Crossref: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets [[2006, 7], [2006, 7]]

title: GPUs make large neural networks practical
one_liner: Graphics cards train networks up to 70 times faster than CPUs.
summary: Raina, Madhavan and Ng showed that graphics processors could speed up unsupervised learning by large factors. GPU training became the norm and later made NVIDIA central to AI.

sources.title: Large-scale deep unsupervised learning using graphics processors

notes: Crossref: Large-scale deep unsupervised learning using graphics processors [[2009, 6, 14], [2009, 6, 14], [2009, 6, 14]]

title: ImageNet: a dataset big enough for deep learning
one_liner: Millions of labelled images, organised by the WordNet hierarchy.
summary: Fei-Fei Li's team built ImageNet with crowd-sourced labels. Its yearly challenge became the benchmark where deep learning first proved itself in 2012.

sources.title: ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database

notes: Crossref: ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database [[2009, 6], [2009, 6]]

title: Google Brain's network learns to spot cats from YouTube
one_liner: A huge network trained on unlabelled video frames learns a 'cat detector' on its own.
summary: Quoc Le, Andrew Ng, Jeff Dean and colleagues trained a billion-connection network on 16,000 CPU cores. Neurons emerged that responded to faces and cats, showing what scale plus unlabelled data could do.

sources.title: Building high-level features using large scale unsupervised learning

notes: arXiv: Building high-level features using large scale unsupervised learning (v1 2011-12-29)

title: AlexNet wins ImageNet by a wide margin
one_liner: A deep convolutional network trained on two GPUs cuts the ImageNet error rate sharply.
summary: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2012 ImageNet challenge with a deep CNN using ReLU, dropout and GPU training. The result convinced the field to switch to deep learning.

sources.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (NeurIPS 2012)

title: word2vec: words as vectors you can do maths with
one_liner: Cheap training gives word vectors where king minus man plus woman lands near queen.
summary: Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google introduced fast methods to learn word embeddings from huge text corpora. Embeddings became a standard building block, and later the core of semantic search and RAG.

title: Deep Q-networks learn Atari games from pixels
one_liner: One network learns to play several Atari games from the screen and the score alone.
summary: DeepMind combined Q-learning with a convolutional network. The same agent learned multiple games from raw pixels, which led Google to acquire DeepMind in 2014.

notes: arXiv: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning (v1 2013-12-19)

title: Variational autoencoders
one_liner: A network that learns a smooth space of possibilities and can sample new data from it.
summary: Kingma and Welling introduced auto-encoding variational Bayes. VAEs became a core generative model and later the image compressor inside latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion.

sources.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

notes: arXiv: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (v1 2013-12-20)

title: Dropout prevents overfitting
one_liner: Randomly switching off neurons during training makes networks generalise better.
summary: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Salakhutdinov published the full dropout paper. It became one of the most used regularisation tricks in deep learning.

sources.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting (JMLR)

title: Generative adversarial networks
one_liner: Two networks compete: one forges images, the other spots forgeries, and both get better.
summary: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced GANs. They produced the first strikingly realistic synthetic images and led to deepfakes, before diffusion models took over image generation.

sources.title: Generative Adversarial Networks

notes: arXiv: Generative Adversarial Networks (v1 2014-06-10)

title: Attention is introduced for translation
one_liner: Instead of squeezing a sentence into one vector, the model looks back at the words it needs.
summary: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio let a translation model learn to align and attend to parts of the input sentence. Attention later became the whole architecture in the transformer.

title: Sequence to sequence learning
one_liner: One LSTM reads a sentence, another writes the translation.
summary: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le showed that an encoder-decoder LSTM could translate end to end. The encoder-decoder pattern carried straight into the original transformer.

sources.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

title: The Adam optimiser
one_liner: A gradient descent method that adapts its step size per parameter.
summary: Kingma and Ba introduced Adam, which combines momentum with adaptive learning rates. Its variants, such as AdamW, train most large models today.

sources.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

notes: arXiv: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (v1 2014-12-22)

title: Batch normalisation
one_liner: Rescaling each layer's inputs makes deep networks train faster and more reliably.
summary: Ioffe and Szegedy introduced batch normalisation, allowing higher learning rates and deeper networks. Later transformers use a cousin, layer normalisation.

title: Google open-sources TensorFlow
one_liner: Google's internal deep learning library becomes free for everyone.
summary: TensorFlow made production-grade deep learning tools available to all developers and helped spread deep learning beyond research labs.

title: ResNet: very deep networks with skip connections
one_liner: Shortcut connections let networks go 150 layers deep and still train.
summary: Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research won ImageNet 2015 with residual networks. Residual connections are inside every transformer layer today.

one_liner: A non-profit AI lab launches with the goal of ensuring AGI benefits everyone.
summary: OpenAI was announced with Ilya Sutskever as research director and Sam Altman and Elon Musk as co-chairs, among others. It later created GPT and ChatGPT.

one_liner: Neural networks plus tree search beat a Go professional, then world champion Lee Sedol in March.

title: Sparsely-gated mixture of experts
one_liner: A giant model where each input only wakes up a few expert sub-networks.
summary: Shazeer, Hinton, Dean and colleagues trained networks with thousands of experts and a learned router. The idea returned in models such as Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3 and many frontier models.

one_liner: Humans compare two behaviours, and the agent learns what they prefer.

title: Attention Is All You Need: the transformer
one_liner: A network built only from attention, which trains in parallel and scales well.

title: Proximal policy optimisation (PPO)
